features.t: VM instances (create, start, stop, suspend, resume, reset, delete)

x: On Nano (in-browser VMs turned on) a Compute Engine instance is a real Linux VM running inside the browser tab (v86, 32-bit x86 Alpine, not the boot image you picked): the SSH section shows its boot state, an xterm.js shell on the VM serial console (root, no tunnel needed) and an ssh command that works only through the local vyomi-tunnel (>= 1.1.0) while the tab is open. Limits: 32-bit x86 only; the VM's RAM is its disk (Stop saves it, Terminate/Delete discards it); a background tab runs the VM several times slower; no general internet egress (only plain-HTTP URLs that allow CORS), so git clone / apt / pip from the internet do not work; the 21 MB image and 2 MB engine load on first launch only. With in-browser VMs off the section offers a Turn on in-browser VMs button and the instance stays a record. Offline uses the Docker-backed SSH described under gcp.compute.instances.data_plane.

features.t: Guest OS access (SSH, screenshot, OS info)
x: SSH (offline): the instance is a real Docker container with sshd. Setting the `ssh-keys` metadata (POST /api/gcp/compute/instances/{id}/ssh-keys, USERNAME:KEY lines) creates the user and authorizes the key in the guest the way the guest agent does, so `ssh -i key user@host -p port` really logs in; malformed lines are rejected. OS info (GET .../os-info) is read from the running guest (os-release, kernel, arch, memory, uptime). OS Login keys use the same path. On Nano, OS info and Screenshot are not simulated; SSH is served by the in-browser VM (see gcp.compute.instances.nano_vm).

Serial output is Vyomi's own instance lifecycle record (create/start/stop/suspend/resume/reset, each at its real timestamp) rendered as console lines, not a real guest kernel's boot/console text — no guest OS runs to produce authentic kernel or init messages.

features.t: Custom images (create from disk, import rawDisk from Cloud Storage, export to Cloud Storage, import/export history)
x: Import (images.insert with rawDisk.source) really checks the .tar.gz object exists in the simulator's Cloud Storage; export writes an image archive (tar.gz with image metadata) into a real destination bucket object. Disk CONTENTS are not modeled, so neither moves guest bytes.

Autoscaling policies aren't simulated — there's no real request load for a policy to react to, so resize (manual, or a rolling update's own batch of creates/deletes) is the only way the member count changes.

features.t: VM Manager (Patch, OS policies, OS inventory, reports, VM extension policies)
x: The OS Config control plane is real: patch jobs (instance filters over the real Compute instances, validation, cancel, per-instance details), patch deployments (schedules, pause/resume, due runs create real patch jobs), OS policy assignments, VM extension policies, OS inventory (instances.inventories) and a fleet patch report.

The status duration and recent-activity feed shown here are real — Vyomi's own recorded instance lifecycle operations (insert/start/stop/suspend/resume/reset/...) at their real timestamps — not Cloud Monitoring charts or Cloud Logging entries: there's no request-metering engine tying a VM's real CPU/disk/network state to a sampled time series (the same boundary as gcp.storage.observability).

Recommendations are computed from live Compute state only (unattached disks, in-use disks without any backup, unused reservations, unattached resource policies, empty sole-tenant node groups). There is no CPU/memory/network utilisation telemetry, so Google's usage-based recommenders (idle VM, rightsizing machine type) are not produced.

Schedules are evaluated lazily on every Compute API call (no background thread in a substrate-independent core): fire times missed while the appliance/browser tab was not running are caught up (last 24 snapshot fires, the most recent start/stop) at the next call instead of firing at their wall-clock minute.

features.t: Snapshot schedules (hourly / daily / weekly with retention)
x: Schedules are evaluated lazily on every Compute API call (no background thread in a substrate-independent core): fire times missed while the appliance/browser tab was not running are caught up (last 24 snapshot fires, the most recent start/stop) at the next call instead of firing at their wall-clock minute.
Instant snapshots are zonal metadata records of a disk (name, source, size); no block data is captured, so a restored disk is an empty disk of the same size.

Replication pairing, constraints (cross-region, size, unattached secondary) and lifecycle are real, but disks hold no block data here, so nothing is copied and there is no measured RPO/replication lag; state is always ACTIVE until stopped.

A consistency group is a diskConsistencyGroupPolicy resource policy attached to disks; group-wide crash-consistent snapshotting and group failover are not performed because no block data is replicated.
Up to 8 NICs in distinct VPC networks are stored and returned (nic0..nicN, per-NIC internal IP); packet forwarding between NICs and per-NIC routing are not simulated (no guest network stack).
The console creates a real VPC firewall rule (130.211.0.0/22, 35.191.0.0/16 on the chosen ports, target tag lb-health-check) and tags the instance; there is no load balancer sending health probes.

Zonal, global (internet) and regional serverless NEGs with endpoint attach/detach/list and validation are real; endpoint health is not reported and a NEG cannot be attached to a backend service because no load balancer data plane exists.

Capacity is not actually held back: reservations are accounting. Running VMs whose machine type and zone match (and whose reservationAffinity allows it) are counted as consumers up to the reserved count, but a VM is never refused for lack of unreserved capacity.

features.t: Sole-tenant nodes (node templates, node groups, node types)
x: Node groups, templates and VM-to-node placement (first-fit by vCPU and memory, with a hard fit check at VM creation) are real; there is no physical host, so maintenance policies and autoscaling are stored but never act, and CPU overcommit is not modelled.

Pool capacity accounting (a disk can't exceed free provisioned capacity; ADVANCED allows 5x thin provisioning) and disk-type matching are enforced; provisioned IOPS/throughput are stored but disks are not throttled by them (there is no I/O path).
Compute rollout plans orchestrate Google-managed product updates across waves; there is no managed fleet or update stream to roll out.

Compute findings are a deterministic rule engine over stored VMs/firewalls. Threat findings come from Vyomi's deterministic detector over the control-plane calls the simulator served (bucket opened to allUsers, Owner/Editor granted, log sink deleted, world-open firewall, KMS destruction, service-account key creation) - no ML threat analysis and no attack-path simulation. Image vulnerabilities come from Artifact Registry scanning (core/vuln_scan_core.py: bundled advisory snapshot + EOL table over the image config; the real Trivy container where the offline appliance has it). It is not Security Command Center: no findings history, muting or org-level aggregation.

features.t: Migrate to Virtual Machines (sources, connectors, migrating VMs, replication cycles, clone/cutover jobs)
x: The vmmigration v1 control plane is real: sources (VMware/AWS/Azure with validation, credentials never echoed), datacenter connectors, migrating VMs with the READY -> FIRST_SYNC -> ACTIVE -> PAUSED/CUTOVER -> FINALIZED state machine, replication cycles, clone jobs and cutover jobs (preconditions enforced), long-running operations. Clone and cutover create a REAL Compute Engine instance (visible in VM instances, offline as a Compute-store record).
The feed reports outages on Google's real infrastructure; Vyomi is a local simulator with no Google status source, so there is nothing true to report.

Record-level Cloud TPU v2 API: nodes create/get/list/patch/delete/start/stop with a CREATING -> READY state machine, accelerator-type and runtime-version catalogues that are zone-aware, and a per-zone, per-generation quota check (RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED). There is no accelerator: nothing can run on a TPU node. Queued resources and TPU pods' networking are not simulated.

features.t: Bare Metal Solution (servers, networks, VRFs, volumes, NFS shares, procurements, maintenance events)
x: Bare Metal Solution provisions physical Oracle-certified servers in a Google-colocated facility with procurement and on-site maintenance workflows; there is no hardware (or meaningful software stand-in) to model.

features.t: Committed use discounts (resource-based and spend-based commitments)
x: Commitments are real records: regionCommitments insert/get/list/aggregatedList with validation (plan, series, vCPU/memory ratio), 1-year/3-year terms, list discounts (37%/55% resource-based, 28%/46% spend-based) and ACTIVE/EXPIRED status from the term. Utilisation and net savings are real arithmetic over the RUNNING instances in the Compute store priced with the cost meter's GCP list prices (core/cost_model.py).

SIMULATED FLEET, NO GOOGLE FLEET DATA. Three tiers: (1) project quota per region for CPUS and the machine family (FAILED / QUOTA_EXCEEDED); (2) an active, unutilised matching reservation (GUARANTEED); (3) a dry-run allocation on a simulated fleet - zone = datacenter, 128-core/512 GB hosts, requested shape = VM, a deterministic per-zone background load that fluctuates over time (HIGH_PROBABILITY, LOW_PROBABILITY or ZONE_RESOURCE_POOL_EXHAUSTED). The probe allocates then deallocates and never consumes capacity. The same pure-Python model runs on Nano and offline (the cloudsim-backbone JVM bridge is not used), so answers are identical for the same state and time.

features.t: Preview features (opt-in to pre-GA Compute Engine features)
x: The catalog and enrollment are managed by Google per project and gate real backend rollouts; Vyomi has a single fixed feature set.

features.t: Instance Observability: Ops Agent host metrics
x: agent.googleapis.com cpu (cpu_state=used only), network and disk series measured inside the instance (cgroup + /proc counters) and pushed to /_obs/gce-counters by a runtime; there is no built-in sampler for GCE instances on this branch, so a VM with no pushes shows 'No samples'. Memory, process and filesystem metrics are not produced.

SSH keys: the instance `ssh-keys` metadata item (and the project one) is real state: lines are validated as USERNAME:ssh-key, shown with SHA256 fingerprints, block-project-ssh-keys is honoured in the effective list. Offline, saving authorizes each key inside the running instance container (guest-agent behaviour) so `ssh -i key user@host -p port` logs in; removing a line does not yet revoke the key already written to the guest. On Nano the metadata is recorded and validated but no guest receives it (SSH there is the in-browser VM).
